newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian bourse cuts operations costs.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian bourse cuts operations costs.

text.p: The Nigerian Stock Exchange (NSE) on Thursday said it was cutting the fees it charged operators as part of its deregulation efforts.
The new fees will be introduced next month, NSE president Pascal Dozie said at the annual general meeting of the bourse.
Details of the new rates were not immediately announced, but the news is certain to cheer operators who have often complained of exhorbitant charges incurred in raising funds in the market.

As part of its move towards liberalisation, the exchange early this year removed the limit on the volume of shares a trader could cross and also introduced a five percent price limit on the daily movement of share prices instead of a former absolute figure.

Attempts to attract foreign portfolio investors since the military government said it internationalised the exchange in 1995 have been frustrated by the absence of the necessary enabling laws and lack of a fast and efficient clearing and settlement system.
Dozie said internationalisation would be further enhanced when its central securities clearing system came into use in the first quarter of 1997.
"The funding problems which had delayed the take off of the project are being resolved partly from our resources and partly from external sources," he said.
But he called on the military government to set up the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission whose job would be to remove difficulties facing interested foreign investors.
The Commission was promised in 1995, but the delay by the government in constituting it is said to be robbing the nation of the benefits of internationalisation.
Dozie, who is chairman of Diamond Bank, said the government should review the suspension of its privatisation programme, saying it was inconsistent with its deregulation policy.

The exchange was criticised by military ruler General Sani Abacha and finance minister Anthony Ani in February for its slow movement towards going international and for not allowing independent exchanges to spring up elsewhere in Nigeria.
A panel was promptly set up to probe its activities as well as the entire capital market. It is due to submit its final report later this month.

The Nigerian Stock Exchange has six branches -- in Lagos, Ibadan, Onitsha, Kaduna, Port Harcourt and Kano. It is to open a seventh in the new capital Abuja. Its market capitalisation is more than 240 billion naira. It grew by 50.3 billion naira, or 29.4 percent, between January and June 1996.
Another four billion naira was added last Monday with the listing of an indigenous bank, Guaranty Trust.
